titre: Alan Freed and the Payola Scandal
accroche: On November 21, 1959, the host who brought the words “rock and roll” to radio is fired from his New York station.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 21, 1959, New York station WABC fires Alan Freed. His offense: refusing to sign a statement denying that he had ever accepted money from a record company to play its songs on the air. Eight years earlier, in July 1951, the same Freed was programming rhythm and blues records on WJW in Cleveland and renaming them “rock and roll,” a term until then confined to slang, to spare them the racial label of the day. On March 21, 1952, his Moondog Coronation Ball, considered the first major rock concert in history, has to be cut short: the crowd far exceeds the capacity of the Cleveland arena.

## An ordinary practice turned affair of state

What is called payola, quietly paying a host to play a record, was no invention of Alan Freed's: it was widespread across the entire American record industry in the 1950s. It becomes an affair of state when the House Subcommittee on Legislative Oversight, already convened that same year over rigged television quiz shows such as *Twenty One*, widens its fall 1959 hearings to the big names of radio. Most of the hosts targeted sign without argument the statement put before them. Freed refuses, never explaining publicly why, and loses his radio show, his television show, and then any chance of being rehired. In December 1962, he finally pleads guilty to two counts of commercial bribery: his sentence is limited to a three-hundred-dollar fine, suspended.

## What it shifts

Before the same committee, host Dick Clark, whose show *American Bandstand* makes him the most profitable figure in televised music promotion, acknowledges holding financial stakes in a large number of record companies, even collecting royalties on nearly one hundred fifty songs he did not write. On orders from his network, ABC, he divests before testifying. He keeps his show, which he will go on hosting for more than thirty years. Freed, for his part, will never again find a stable job and dies in January 1965, at forty-three, of the effects of alcoholism.

Payola therefore did not separate corrupt hosts from honest ones: Clark was, on paper, far more deeply involved financially than Freed. What decided the outcome was cooperation, not degree of fault. The first cut his exposure in time; the second, already accused of promoting the “mixing of the races” on stage by booking Black artists before mixed audiences, refused to sign a piece of paper, and history remembered his name as that of the scandal, while Clark's faded away.

repere.texte: In December 1962, Alan Freed pleads guilty to two counts of commercial bribery; his sentence is limited to a three-hundred-dollar fine, suspended.

carte.punch: He brought the words “rock and roll” to radio. He dies at 43, with no steady job.
carte.idee: In 1959, Alan Freed refuses to sign a statement denying that he took money from record companies to play their songs. He loses everything. Dick Clark, far more heavily invested in the industry, cooperates and keeps his show for thirty more years.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full course of the 1959-1960 hearings and their regulatory aftermath.

quiz.question: Why was Alan Freed fired when payola was a widespread practice across the whole record industry?
choix: Because he had accepted more money than other radio hosts
Because federal law had already explicitly banned payola since the 1930s
Because he refused to sign the statement denying any payment, unlike most of his colleagues
Because a journalist had published proof of direct payments to his home
quiz.explication: Nothing indicates that Freed took more money than his colleagues, and payola was not yet a distinct federal offense before the 1959 hearings. It was his refusal to sign the clearing statement, when most hosts signed it, that led to his firing: no journalistic investigation was behind the affair.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Alan Freed do in 1951 on station WJW in Cleveland?
choix: He organized the first major rock and roll concert in history
He signed his first advertising contract with a record company
He was fired for the first time for refusing to cooperate with a committee
He programmed rhythm and blues records that he renamed “rock and roll”
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In July 1951, on WJW in Cleveland, Freed programs rhythm and blues records that he renames “rock and roll” to spare them the racial label of the day, a year before the Moondog Coronation Ball.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Dick Clark avoid the fate dealt to Alan Freed before the same investigative committee?
choix: By proving he had never received money from a record company
By divesting his financial stakes in the record industry before testifying
By resigning from his show before the hearings opened
By publicly accusing Alan Freed of being solely responsible for payola
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On orders from the ABC network, Clark divests his financial stakes and his royalties on nearly one hundred fifty songs before testifying, then keeps his show for more than thirty years.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What other accusation was leveled at Alan Freed even before the payola scandal?
choix: Promoting the “mixing of the races” by booking Black artists before mixed audiences
Falsifying the record sales of his artists
Plagiarizing the term “rock and roll” coined by another host
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that Freed was already accused of promoting the “mixing of the races” on stage, by booking Black artists before mixed audiences, even before the payola scandal.
